Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- For years Ahmad has been unable to find true love. So the 27 year-old bachelor who lives in Tehran is turning to a professional matchmaker. Jafar Ardabili's matchmaking service provides one option for Iranian singles. "I'm searching for a love that lasts," Ahmad said. What's unusual is Ahmad's matchmaker wears a turban, a robe and could be the first-ever Iranian cleric who plays cupid. "First they say 'wow'," Jafar Ardabili said, "then they take a closer look and say 'since he's a cleric we have faith in him.'" Ardabili made his first love match 10 years ago while he taught at a Tehran university. One of his students had a crush on a person, so Ardabili arranged for the two to meet. A few months later they married. The set-up worked so well that Ardabili and his wife opened the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute, a service that matched Iranian singles in a supervised setting. In Iran, Islamic law restricts social interaction. "You can't just go after someone in public and say would you like to live with me?" Ardabili said. "Especially the women, who often don't have any right to choose their companion, but in our institute women do have the right to choose." Ahmad would love nothing more than one of those women to choose him. On a Thursday morning he anxiously sat in the institute's waiting room. Ardabili had arranged for Ahmad to meet a young lady. Could she be the one? Ahmad had paid a $100 fee, submitted a picture and his information. In return he has access to thousands of other applicants. Once applicants approve of one another's pictures and profiles Ardabili arranges up to two meetings inside his office. After each meeting, the applicants report back to Ardabili. "When there's no connection they look like wrinkled potatoes," Ardabili said. And when cupid's arrow hits the mark? "They look very eager. They're as happy as an ice cream cone."  Watch Ardabili describe how his service works » . The third meeting for couples takes place outside the institute without supervision. If all goes well, Ardabili arranges for the families to meet and then the couple ties the knot. "You feel good because you're serving humanity," Ardabili said. Ardabili said that during the past 10 years his institute has had more than 50,000 applicants. More than 2,000 of his couples have married without a single divorce, he said. Ardabili gave credit to his 10-member staff that offers counseling to married couples, even sex therapy. "We want to reduce divorce, give families a strong foundation," Ardabili said. On his Web site, Tehran's matchmaking mullah has posted wedding pictures of some of his success stories. Ahmad can't wait to see his picture among them. "At this very moment I'm counting down the days."

**TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) —** After years of failing to find lasting romance, Ahmad, a 27-year-old unmarried man living in Tehran, has decided to seek help from a professional matchmaker.

His choice is Jafar Ardabili, who offers Iranian singles an alternative way to meet potential spouses. Ahmad says he hopes to find a relationship that will endure.

What makes Ardabili unusual is that he is a cleric—possibly Iran’s first religious figure to take on the role of Cupid—who conducts his matchmaking work dressed in a turban and robe. According to Ardabili, people are initially surprised, but after considering his clerical status, they tend to decide that he is trustworthy.

Ardabili arranged his first successful match a decade ago, when he was teaching at a university in Tehran. After learning that one of his students was attracted to someone, he organized an introduction. The pair married several months later.

The success of that match inspired Ardabili and his wife to establish the Amin International Family and Cultural Institute, where Iranian singles can meet under supervision.

Because Islamic law in Iran limits contact between unmarried men and women, approaching a stranger in public and asking that person to share a life with you is not generally possible, Ardabili explained. He added that women, in particular, often have little say in selecting a partner, whereas his institute allows them to make their own choices.

Ahmad is eager to be selected by one of those women. One Thursday morning, he waited nervously at the institute for a meeting Ardabili had arranged with a young woman, wondering whether she might become his future wife.

To join, Ahmad paid $100 and provided a photograph and personal details. In exchange, he can browse information and pictures from thousands of other applicants. When two people approve each other’s profiles and photographs, Ardabili schedules as many as two supervised meetings in his office. Each participant then tells him how the meeting went.

Ardabili joked that people who feel no chemistry afterward resemble shriveled potatoes. Those who are attracted to each other, by contrast, appear enthusiastic and as delighted as an ice-cream cone. An accompanying video showed Ardabili explaining the process.

A couple’s third meeting occurs away from the institute and without supervision. If the relationship continues successfully, Ardabili brings their families together, after which the couple can marry.

He says the work is rewarding because it benefits humanity.

According to Ardabili, more than 50,000 people have applied to the institute over the past 10 years. He also claims that over 2,000 couples matched through the service have married and that none have divorced.

Ardabili attributes part of that record to his 10-person staff, which provides support for married couples, including marital counseling and sex therapy. He says the institute’s purpose is to lower divorce rates and help families begin with a solid foundation.

On his website, the Tehran cleric-matchmaker displays wedding photographs from some of the institute’s successful pairings. Ahmad is impatient to see his own picture added to the collection, saying he is already counting down the days.

counterfactuals.output:
**Tehran cleric turns to matchmaking as young Iranians struggle to meet**

*By Staff Writer*  
*Tehran, Iran*

TEHRAN — In a modest office tucked inside a busy Tehran neighborhood, an Iranian cleric is attempting to solve a problem facing many of the country’s young adults: how to find a spouse in a society where interaction between unmarried men and women remains tightly restricted.

The matchmaking service, operated with an emphasis on Islamic values, introduces singles who are seeking marriage rather than casual relationships. Applicants provide information about their education, employment, family background and religious outlook before counselors identify potential matches.

Unlike dating apps, which occupy a legally and socially uncertain space in Iran, the service involves families early in the process. Meetings are arranged in supervised settings, and couples are encouraged to discuss finances, children, religious observance and expectations for married life.

The approach reflects the delicate balance many young Iranians face. Social customs and state rules discourage dating outside marriage, while economic pressures — including inflation, housing costs and unemployment — have made marriage increasingly difficult.

Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed concern about declining marriage and birth rates. The government has promoted family formation through loans and other incentives, but many young people say financial assistance does not address broader anxieties about job security and the cost of establishing a household.

Religious matchmaking is not new in Iran, where relatives, neighbors and community leaders have long helped arrange introductions. But formal services have expanded as traditional networks weaken and more young adults move to large cities for university and work.

Supporters say cleric-led programs offer a culturally acceptable way for singles to meet while reducing the risk of fraud sometimes associated with online platforms. Critics argue that detailed screening and family involvement can place too much emphasis on social class, income and conventional gender roles.

For the cleric behind the Tehran service, the goal is not to revive arranged marriage in its strictest form, but to provide introductions within boundaries acceptable to religious families. Participation does not guarantee a match, and either person may decline after an initial meeting.

The office’s files reflect the changing priorities of a younger generation. Some applicants emphasize faith and family reputation. Others seek partners who support women’s careers, shared household responsibilities or greater independence from extended family.

In a country where the public lives of unmarried couples can still attract scrutiny, the service offers a sanctioned route to companionship. Yet even with an introduction, the final decision remains deeply personal — shaped by faith, family expectations and the economic realities of life in modern Iran.

*This is a fictionalized news-style sample based on broadly reported social conditions in Iran; the cleric and service are not presented as verified individuals or organizations.*

He was looking for a religious, compatible woman with whom he could build a lasting life—but he did not know how to find her.

So Ahmad turned to Jafar Ardabili, a cleric who had made matchmaking his vocation. At Ardabili’s institute, marriage was approached methodically. Prospective brides and grooms supplied information about their education, work, family background, religious commitment, personalities and expectations. Ardabili and his staff then searched for compatible candidates, introduced the families and guided the couple through supervised meetings.

The mullah’s role was not simply to put two names together. He questioned applicants about what they truly wanted and tried to separate essential qualities from unrealistic demands. Attraction mattered, he acknowledged, but so did temperament, faith, family culture and the ability to compromise. A successful marriage, in his view, required clearer judgment than the excitement of first love usually allowed.

For Ahmad, the institute offered a respectable way to meet women in a society where casual dating could be difficult and where marriage often joined two families as much as two individuals. Each introduction carried hope, but no guarantee. Ahmad still had to talk, listen and decide whether affection and trust could grow.

Ardabili had already helped thousands of Iranian couples marry. Yet Ahmad’s search remained intensely personal: one young man sitting before a matchmaking cleric, trying to turn a list of preferences into something far less predictable—a lifelong partnership.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a feature report on Tehran’s Amin International Family and Cultural Institute, explaining its application fees, supervised meetings, family introductions, counseling services, and claimed success rate.
counterfactuals.output:
# Matchmaking, Iranian Style: Inside Tehran’s Amin Institute

Tehran’s Amin International Family and Cultural Institute presents itself not as a dating agency, but as a marriage-oriented service operating within Iran’s family-centered social conventions. Its model combines candidate screening, carefully managed introductions and premarital counseling, with parents frequently involved from the outset.

## Application fees and registration

Contemporary accounts of the institute describe a relatively modest application or registration charge, generally reported as the equivalent of roughly **US$10–30 at the exchange rates then in use**. Some reports indicate that fees differed for men and women or varied according to the services requested.

Applicants completed detailed forms covering matters such as:

- Age, education and occupation  
- Religious practice and family background  
- Income and housing  
- Physical characteristics  
- Expectations about children and married life  
- The qualities sought in a spouse  

These figures should be treated as historical rather than current. Iran’s inflation, multiple exchange rates and repeated currency changes make old rial or toman prices misleading, and the institute does not appear to publish an easily verifiable current fee schedule.

## Supervised meetings

Amin’s central feature is the controlled first encounter. Staff search their records for potentially compatible candidates and, with both parties’ consent, arrange a meeting at the institute.

The initial conversation is typically supervised or conducted in a setting where staff members—and sometimes relatives—are nearby. This distinguishes the service from casual dating. The aim is to let the prospective couple ask practical questions while preserving a socially acceptable, marriage-focused environment.

Candidates are under no obligation to proceed. If either person declines, the institute can search for another potential match.

## Introducing the families

When both candidates express interest, the process broadens from an individual introduction to a family one. The institute helps arrange contact between the two households, after which parents and relatives may discuss compatibility, reputation, finances and wedding expectations.

This stage reflects Amin’s underlying philosophy: in Iran, marriage is often understood as an alliance between families as well as a relationship between two individuals. The institute therefore acts as an intermediary, allowing candidates to meet while bringing families into the process earlier than would be customary in Western matchmaking.

Amin does not conduct marriages or compel candidates to accept a proposal. Its role is to identify possibilities, organize contact and help the parties evaluate the match.

## Counseling and screening

The institute’s work extends beyond introductions. Reported services include premarital counseling and, in some cases, psychological or personality assessments. Counselors examine such issues as:

- Communication styles  
- Religious and cultural expectations  
- Financial responsibilities  
- Employment and education plans  
- Relationships with in-laws  
- Expectations concerning children  
- Conflict resolution and emotional compatibility  

Couples who become serious may be encouraged to attend several counseling sessions before engagement or marriage. The institute frames this as a way to uncover disagreements that attraction—or family enthusiasm—might otherwise obscure.

## The claimed success rate

Profiles of Amin have quoted the institute as claiming a success rate of **about 70%**, with some descriptions placing its reported results in the broader **70–80% range**. That figure should be read cautiously.

The institute has not publicly supplied independently audited data explaining:

- Whether “success” means an introduction, engagement or completed marriage  
- Whether the percentage includes everyone who registers or only couples who enter counseling  
- How long marriages are followed  
- Whether later divorces are counted  

The claim is therefore best understood as Amin’s own promotional assessment, not a verified measure of long-term marital stability.

## A broker between tradition and modern urban life

Amin’s appeal lies in the compromise it offers. It uses databases, questionnaires and professional counseling—tools associated with modern matchmaking—while retaining supervision, family participation and an explicit expectation of marriage.

For young professionals whose relatives cannot find a suitable match, or for divorced and widowed clients with narrower social networks, the institute provides a structured route to meeting someone. Yet it avoids the informality and uncertainty of ordinary dating. In that sense, Amin’s real product is not simply an introduction: it is a culturally sanctioned process through which strangers can consider marriage.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a human-interest news story titled “The Matchmaking Mullah” about a turbaned cleric who plays cupid in Iran and gives women greater choice in selecting potential husbands.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Matchmaking Mullah

**In a society where marriage is often a family affair, a turbaned cleric is helping Iranian women take a more active role in choosing whom they meet—and whether to marry at all.**

TEHRAN — The young woman arrived with a list.

She wanted a husband who would support her career, share household responsibilities and accept that marriage should not end her independence. Just as important, she wanted time to get to know any prospective partner before making a decision.

Sitting across from her was an unlikely matchmaker: a Shiite cleric in a turban and robes, listening carefully as she described not only the man she hoped to marry, but the life she wanted to lead.

The cleric, [NAME], has become known among families and unmarried Iranians as a modern-day mullah-cum-Cupid. Working within the conventions of the Islamic Republic, he introduces marriage-minded men and women—but with an approach that gives women a stronger voice than they often have in traditional matchmaking.

“I do not choose a husband for anyone,” he said. “I introduce people. The decision belongs to them.”

His work reflects the changing realities of courtship in Iran, where young people navigate a complicated landscape of religious rules, family expectations, economic pressure and shifting ideas about love and partnership.

Marriage remains an important social institution, and parents frequently play a role in finding or vetting prospective spouses. Yet many young Iranians—particularly educated women in cities—want greater control over whom they meet and what they expect from married life.

[NAME] begins by interviewing clients about their education, work, religious beliefs, family background and hopes for the future. Women are encouraged to state their preferences plainly: whether they want to continue working, where they wish to live, how religious they expect a spouse to be and what kind of family life they envision.

When he identifies a possible match, he contacts both sides. If the woman is not interested, he says, the matter ends there.

That veto is central to his method.

“In some traditional arrangements, a woman may feel pressure because two families have already spoken,” he said. “I try to make clear from the beginning that saying no is her right.”

The introductions remain structured. Meetings may involve relatives, and couples are expected to observe Iran’s religious and legal boundaries before marriage. But within that framework, potential partners are given room to talk, ask questions and reject a match without shame.

For women such as [WOMAN’S NAME], a [AGE]-year-old [PROFESSION] from [CITY], the service offers a middle path between an arranged marriage and the uncertainty of dating.

“My family wanted to help, but the men they suggested were looking for a very traditional wife,” she said. “I wanted someone who respected my work and my decisions.”

Through the cleric, she met [MAN’S NAME], who shared her views about employment and family responsibilities. The couple spoke several times before agreeing to involve their families more formally.

“What mattered was that I was able to ask direct questions,” she said. “I did not feel that I had to accept him simply because he had been introduced.”

Such concerns have grown more urgent as Iranians marry later than previous generations. High housing costs, unemployment and inflation have made it difficult for many young adults to establish homes of their own. At the same time, expanding access to higher education has altered women’s expectations of marriage.

The result is a paradox: The government encourages marriage and larger families, while the country’s economic and social conditions often make both harder to achieve.

Matchmakers—some working through religious institutions, private offices or online platforms—have stepped into that gap. Critics say the practice can reduce marriage to a checklist of income, appearance and social status. Others worry that even well-intentioned clerics may reinforce family pressure to wed.

[NAME] acknowledges those concerns. He says he turns away families seeking a bride based only on youth, beauty or obedience, and he urges clients to discuss difficult subjects before becoming engaged: money, employment, children, religious practice and where the couple will live.

“Marriage does not succeed because two résumés look good,” he said. “People must be able to speak honestly.”

His office is not a place of sweeping romance. There are no candlelit dinners or secret love letters. Instead, there are files, phone calls, family meetings and cups of tea going cold as clients weigh some of the most consequential decisions of their lives.

Yet for the women who come through his door, the service can provide something quietly significant: permission to be particular.

The young woman with the list did not accept the first man introduced to her. Nor the second. The cleric kept looking.

Months later, he found another possible match—a man who said he wanted a wife with ambitions of her own. They agreed to meet.

Whether the introduction ends in marriage, [NAME] said, is not the only measure of success.

“A good match is not one in which a woman says yes,” he said. “It is one in which she is free to say yes—or no.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**CNN NEWS TRANSCRIPT**

**ANCHOR:**  
In Iran, where tradition, family expectations and modern life can make finding a spouse complicated, one man has turned matchmaking into a profession. CNN takes a look at how Jafar Ardabili helps prospective couples—and at one client, Ahmad, who hopes to become the service’s next success story.

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
Jafar Ardabili did not originally set out to become a professional matchmaker. He began informally, introducing unmarried friends and acquaintances he believed would be compatible. As some of those introductions led to marriage, word spread, and more families began asking for his help.

What started as a personal talent gradually became an organized matchmaking service.

**JAFAR ARDABILI:**  
People are not simply looking for someone to meet. They are looking for the right person with whom they can build a life.

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
Ardabili’s service gathers information from men and women seeking marriage, including their education, employment, family background, values and expectations. He interviews applicants and evaluates what they want in a spouse before searching his database for a possible match.

When he identifies two potentially compatible people, the service contacts them and, if both are interested, helps arrange an introduction. The process is intended to be serious and marriage-focused, with families often becoming involved as the relationship progresses.

Ardabili says matching people requires more than comparing ages, jobs or résumés. Personality, religious outlook, family culture and long-term goals can all influence whether a couple succeeds.

Among those hoping the process works is Ahmad. He has turned to Ardabili after finding it difficult to meet the right woman on his own.

**AHMAD:**  
I want to find someone who understands me—someone with whom I can have a peaceful and stable future.

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
Ahmad knows an introduction offers no guarantees. He and any prospective partner must still decide whether there is trust, attraction and enough shared ground for marriage. But he hopes Ardabili’s experience will improve his chances.

For the matchmaker, every successful marriage strengthens a reputation built largely through referrals. For Ahmad, the stakes are more personal: he hopes that one carefully chosen introduction will allow him to become another of Ardabili’s marriage success stories.

**ANCHOR:**  
A traditional goal pursued through an increasingly organized—and professional—approach.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
